The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (the Alliance) is set to hear its verdict on a charge of inciting subversion of state power on 21 August, with Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, who did not plead guilty, having been in custody for nearly five years over the case. The prosecution alleges that the Alliance's slogan "End one-party dictatorship", chanted for over 30 years, is tantamount to "ending the leadership of the Communist Party" and overthrowing or undermining the fundamental system of the state, constituting incitement to subvert state power by "illegal means". The defence countered that "End one-party dictatorship" merely calls for ending an unlawful "party dictatorship" and building a democratic China, which is not the same as ending the Communist Party's leadership; the defendants bear no hostility towards the Communist Party and have no subversive intent, while the prosecution has failed to identify what action the Alliance encouraged people to take to "end one-party dictatorship". What exactly are the prosecution's allegations? How did the defence rebut them? How did the court handle disputes over the Chinese Constitution and the Tiananmen crackdown? On the eve of the verdict, HK Featurepress has compiled nine key points and controversies from the 24-day trial. Related coverage of the Alliance case

The Alliance, its chair Lee Cheuk-yan, vice-chairs Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung have been charged with incitement to subvert state power, with the verdict scheduled for 21 August.

控方的檢控基礎是什麼？

The Alliance, Lee Cheuk-yan, Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung are charged with "incitement to subvert state power", alleging that they incited others in Hong Kong to commit acts "aimed at subverting state power" by "illegal means", namely overthrowing or undermining the fundamental system of the state established by the Chinese Constitution, or overthrowing the central authorities. The prosecution defined "illegal means" as "ending the leadership of the Communist Party of China in violation of the Chinese Constitution (in particular Article 1 and the Preamble)", treating so-called "acts in violation of the Chinese Constitution" as "illegal".

At the core of the allegations is "End one-party dictatorship", one of the Alliance's five major goals. The prosecution argued that the Alliance promoted and disseminated the "End one-party dictatorship" stance under the guise of "so-called democracy or the Tiananmen incident", combining it with negative content targeting the state. While there was no explicit or detailed plan, the "natural and reasonable effect" of this stance was to "end the leadership of the Communist Party of China".

The prosecution's core allegation centres on "End one-party dictatorship", one of the Alliance's five major goals, which it claimed is tantamount to ending the Communist Party's leadership.

The prosecution's logic is that Article 1 of the Chinese Constitution, as amended in 2018, stipulates that "the socialist system is the fundamental system of the People's Republic of China. The leadership of the Communist Party of China is the defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics. No organisation or individual may undermine the socialist system". This reflects that the Communist Party's leadership is the "fundamental system of the state established by the Constitution", and there is "no legal means whatsoever" to end it. Therefore, the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" must constitute incitement to subvert state power by "illegal means" in violation of the Chinese Constitution.

However, this basis of prosecution was rejected by the court at the mid-point of submissions. The judges considered the matter significant and far-reaching, but found the prosecution's submissions "superficial", lacking sufficient analysis and supporting literature, and without expert testimony, and would not consider it. The court would only consider the prosecution's second basis of prosecution: even if there were legal means to end the Communist Party's leadership, the Alliance was in substance not advocating constitutional amendment, but inciting people to use unlawful means to overthrow the Communist Party's leading position.

法庭應如何詮釋中國憲法？

As the elements of the charge involve the Chinese Constitution, how the court should interpret and apply the relevant provisions became crucial. No expert on the Chinese Constitution was called to testify in the case. Chow Hang-tung pointed out that the power of constitutional interpretation rests with the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, and Hong Kong courts have no authority to interpret the Constitution. Furthermore, Hong Kong lawyers and judges are trained in common law and lack relevant expertise. In the absence of expert evidence and without consensus between prosecution and defence, the court should not even interpret the constitutional provisions literally.

The prosecution agreed that Hong Kong courts have no authority to interpret the Constitution, but argued that the wording is very clear and can be understood and applied literally without expert assistance. Lee Cheuk-yan's team also considered that the court could interpret the provisions literally, but if the prosecution made submissions beyond the literal meaning, expert evidence would be required; otherwise, such submissions should not be accepted.

The judge ultimately ruled that for constitutional provisions that can be directly applied in Hong Kong and are relevant to the case, including the Preamble and Article 1 relied upon by the prosecution, the court could understand their plain meaning based on the literal text and context as the basis for its determination, but could not rely on meanings beyond the literal text.

The elements of the charge involve the Chinese Constitution, and the prosecution did not call any expert to testify. The judge ruled that the plain meaning of the relevant provisions could be understood based on the literal text and context.

如何處理六四等政治議題？是非曲直是否相關？

As the Alliance is charged, political subjects such as the Tiananmen crackdown inevitably entered the courtroom. In its opening statement, the prosecution made clear that this was not a political trial, and did not involve adjudicating any matters concerning democracy, the Tiananmen massacre, criticism of the state, or the merits or demerits of historical or political systems. Whether the state constitution is democratic as the defendants claimed, or the negative content alleged by the prosecution, was "fundamentally irrelevant to the case and the court need not address it".

However, the prosecution simultaneously alleged that the defendants exploited current affairs issues to incite, using negative content to arouse hatred toward the regime and strengthen the inciting effect, and used Tiananmen vigils and the June Fourth Memorial Museum to disseminate the "End one-party dictatorship" stance. The judge at one point quipped that the prosecution was saying the Alliance was "selling dog meat under the guise of selling mutton", but the prosecution denied this, saying "we did not say their claims were false" and they "could be true"; the point was the use of these events to provoke hatred of the Communist Party, achieving the goal of overthrowing the Communist Party's leadership.

The prosecution alleged that the defendants exploited current affairs issues to incite, using the "June Fourth Memorial Museum" and other means to disseminate their stance.

The prosecution's claims were denied by the defence. Lee Cheuk-yan said the Alliance's actions were all protests against specific events, such as Liu Xiaobo's imprisonment, Liu Xia's house arrest, the 709 crackdown, and the alleged suicide of Li Wangyang, and not smears under the guise of democracy. Chow Hang-tung emphasised that the Tiananmen massacre was a real event, not fabricated or slanderous of the government. The focus of the Tiananmen vigils was mourning, and the Memorial Museum was for preserving and transmitting the truth. To claim it was set up to advocate the Charter was putting the cart before the horse: "The June Fourth massacre has never been a tool we used to incite 'End one-party dictatorship'... it is lives, it is blood, it is a crime the government must face, not a tool that can be exploited."

When Chow Hang-tung sought to call witnesses to testify about what happened on June Fourth, the judge repeatedly interrupted and stopped her, emphasising that the court would not judge the rights and wrongs of the Tiananmen massacre. Chow countered that the prosecution alleged the defendants had smeared and fabricated falsehoods, and therefore basic factual determinations were needed to judge whether the allegations were true. If it could be established that the Alliance spoke facts and made reasonable demands, this would fall within the scope of freedom of speech. However, the judge reiterated that the court had no way of determining whether such things were true, stressing that this case was not about June Fourth but whether the National Security Law had been violated, and "I will not allow you to use this opportunity for political propaganda".

Politics cannot be discussed, yet the prosecution used political reasoning to infer the defendants' intent. Lee Cheuk-yan's team noted in closing that if the court did not address the relevant issues and could not judge whether the criticism was justified, it should not conclude that the defendants had used these issues to smear or cause hatred of the Communist Party.

Chow Hang-tung emphasised that the Tiananmen massacre was a real event, saying June Fourth "is lives, it is blood", not a tool that can be exploited.

「結束一黨專政」等於「結束共產黨領導」？等於「推翻、破壞國家根本制度」？

The core of the prosecution's allegations is essentially a chain of equations: "End one-party dictatorship" = "End the Communist Party's leadership" = "Overthrow or undermine the fundamental system of the state". The defendants admitted they persisted in "End one-party dictatorship", but rejected the equation with "ending the Communist Party's leadership".

Lee Cheuk-yan explained that the Alliance hoped to end the dictatorship, not the Communist Party's leadership. Dictatorship and democracy are opposites, and "End one-party dictatorship" meant hoping the people would enjoy fundamental rights and a civil society could be established, providing a basis for discussing democracy, after which the people would decide whether the Communist Party should continue to lead. "Whether the Communist Party leads or not is not for us to say, but for the people to say." He also cited statements from successive national leaders in support, such as Mao Zedong's promise not to practise one-party dictatorship after the founding of the PRC, and Zhao Ziyang's remark that the Communist Party could not monopolise governance.

Lee Cheuk-yan cited remarks from successive national leaders during his testimony, such as Mao Zedong's promise not to practise one-party dictatorship after the founding of the state, and Zhao Ziyang's point that the Communist Party could not monopolise power.

Chow Hang-tung pointed out that "one-party dictatorship" refers to a power structure, while "the Communist Party's leadership" refers to the actual power of a certain group; the two concepts are different and cannot be compared. "End one-party dictatorship" is a demand to return power to the people and end the state where the Party stands above the law. It is not equivalent to "ending the Communist Party's leadership", but rather to "building a democratic China".

The prosecution questioned the defendants, arguing that calling for "End one-party dictatorship" meant demanding a change of ruling party, a "change of dynasty". Both defendants reiterated that the position was for the people to decide whether the Communist Party should govern, and party rotation in a democratic system was commonplace.

Even if "End one-party dictatorship" were equivalent to "ending the Communist Party's leadership", the defence rejected the equation with "overthrowing or undermining" the fundamental system of the state. The defence argued that "overthrow" implies violent, forceful, or abnormal means of drastically changing the order, and "end" does not imply overthrowing. For 30 years, the Alliance had worked to promote human rights through persistent effort; simply advocating a slogan without any concrete action could not be called "overthrowing". "Undermining" carries malicious intent, but the Alliance appealed to facts and exercised civil rights. Even if this hurt the Communist Party's leading position, it did not constitute "undermining".

The defence also challenged the claim that Communist Party leadership is the fundamental system of the state. Chow Hang-tung pointed out that the Constitution does not literally grant the Communist Party any actual power; the prosecution's claim that the Communist Party dominates everything merely reflects political reality. There is only one fundamental system of the state, namely the socialist system, which can encompass various elements. When interpreting the Constitution, the founding principles must be considered, and the meaning cannot be derived from the text alone. She argued that since the court had already restricted itself to a literal interpretation of the Constitution, it could not determine whether the prosecution's interpretation was correct; and if the fundamental principle of the Constitution is democratic constitutionalism, calling for an end to one-party dictatorship could not be unconstitutional.

Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan's team repeatedly pointed out that the prosecution had never specified what action the Alliance encouraged people to take to "end one-party dictatorship".

被告有否煽動人用「非法手段」？控方如何確立被告用「非法手段」？

The prosecution's basis of prosecution is that the Alliance was not advocating constitutional amendment, but inciting people to use "illegal means" to overthrow the Communist Party's leadership. "Illegal means" is an important element of the charge in the case. The defence argued this was the "fatal flaw" of the prosecution, as it had never been able to specify what action the Alliance encouraged people to take to "end one-party dictatorship".

Lee Cheuk-yan testified that he supported "End one-party dictatorship" but did not call on people to take action: "We would not say 'go do something to end one-party dictatorship'." What they called on people to do were concrete actions, such as signing petitions demanding the release of Liu Xiaobo, or sending Christmas cards to prisoners. Chow Hang-tung also pointed out that the Tiananmen vigils, the Memorial Museum, and human rights advocacy work have their own intrinsic purposes and meanings; they were the practice of the five major goals, not inciting others to do anything. Lee Cheuk-yan's team concluded that the Alliance served a supportive and educational role, and noted that if the Alliance had truly incited people to take concrete action, it would have been "a real failure", because in 30 years, regardless of how many people participated in rallies and marches, no single thing in Hong Kong had actually been carried out under the Alliance's impetus to end one-party dictatorship.

Chow Hang-tung also emphasised that one-party dictatorship is a power structure, not rule by a particular party, and can only be ended through democratic and lawful means. Ordinary people can only take indirect approaches, such as collecting and preserving evidence, public education and empowerment, and pressure through public opinion, attempting to break the monopoly from the bottom up. She cited Albert Ho's article "How to End One-Party Dictatorship", which mentioned three paths: self-reform by leaders, violent revolution, and peaceful civil resistance. The Alliance rejected violent revolution and had for years engaged in peaceful resistance. For example, it had submitted reports to the UN Human Rights Council addressing human rights issues in mainland China and made various recommendations to the Chinese government, all calling for the use of the rule of law and legal means to end one-party dictatorship: "We advocated that the thief should return what he stole, but we never advocated beating up the thief to take it back."

Chow Hang-tung once called a housewife, Shum Lai-fong, to testify. She said she had participated in the Tiananmen candlelight vigils and the late-May march as a citizen, with the purpose of mourning the dead.

The prosecution also questioned why the defendants had never mentioned constitutional amendment; however, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung said they supported the democratic movement, including constitutional amendment, and the Alliance's support for Charter 08 also reflected the aspiration for legal constitutional amendment.

Regarding the prosecution's claim that the "natural and reasonable effect" of the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" was to overthrow the Communist Party's leadership, Chow Hang-tung rebutted that the natural and reasonable effect of actions like street stalls was to call on people to attend gatherings. Mentioning "End one-party dictatorship" during the process would not magically transform it into encouraging people to do "some unknown act that is both unconstitutional and can end one-party dictatorship". The citizen witness she called also testified that over the years they had attended the vigils to mourn the dead, not because they agreed with the five major goals and wanted to do something. Lee Cheuk-yan's team argued that Hong Kong people "are not fools" and should not be assumed to understand "End one-party dictatorship" in the same way as the prosecution.

Regarding the prosecution's definition of "illegal means" as "unconstitutional means", Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung stressed that the Constitution constrains the government, not the people, and they did not believe ordinary people could violate the Constitution. The defence criticised the prosecution for "circular reasoning": defining means violating Article 1 of the Constitution as illegal means, and then claiming the subversive goal of "ending the Communist Party's leadership" violates Article 1 of the Constitution—in other words, using "unconstitutionality" to prove both the goal and the means simultaneously, which is tantamount to accusing the defendants of "violating Article 22 of the National Security Law by means that violate Article 22 of the National Security Law".

被告有否煽動顛覆意圖？

The prosecution in this case had to prove "dual intent", meaning that the defendants not only intended to incite others to commit subversive acts, but also intended to incite subversion. The prosecution inferred subversive intent from the defendants' hostility towards the Communist Party; the defence rejected this, stressing that the goal was to build a democratic China, not to subvert.

Lee Cheuk-yan, when cross-examined, agreed that he considered the Communist Party an authoritarian regime that suppressed the people and strangled democracy, but disagreed that he bore great hostility towards the Communist Party, saying "there is no hostility in my heart, only love". He said his criticism was based on love for the people, hoping the Communist Party could reform so that the people would receive their due rights. He professed himself "absolutely patriotic", hoping the country would be democratic, prosperous, and free, and the people would have a good future. The defence stressed that the prosecution had no evidence that Lee Cheuk-yan was "not speaking his mind".

Chow Hang-tung reiterated that advocating "End one-party dictatorship" meant subverting an unlawful party dictatorship, demanding accountability from those in power and "returning power to the people". She said the current charge was "like us, as the masters of the country, telling a thief to return what he stole, only for the thief to accuse us of robbery". The judge once asked if she was placing the Communist Party in an adversarial position, and she said she would not use the word "enemy": "As Mr Liu Xiaobo said, we have no enemies. What we resist is the system."

Chow Hang-tung said she would not use the word "enemy" to describe the Communist Party, citing Liu Xiaobo: "We have no enemies. What we resist is the system."

是否明知「結束一黨專政」違法？

The prosecution alleged that the defendants, knowing "End one-party dictatorship" was unlawful after the National Security Law came into effect, persisted in it. The defence denied this outright. Lee Cheuk-yan said he "believed he was completely not breaking the law" at the time, noting that for over 30 years no one had ever said there was a problem with "End one-party dictatorship". After the National Security Law, no one or police had ever said the slogan violated the National Security Law, or banned the Alliance's operations on national security grounds. The 2021 Tiananmen vigil was banned on the grounds of the pandemic, not national security.

Chow Hang-tung acknowledged that the Alliance had discussed how to respond to the National Security Law, but believed that "fighting for democracy cannot be illegal" and the risk was also "unavoidable". The final consensus was to adhere to the five major goals. The judge noted that they were aware of legal risks at the time, but Chow disagreed, saying she believed there was no legal violation but political risk, as the National Security Law could be used as a tool for political suppression.

Chow Hang-tung acknowledged that after the implementation of the National Security Law, the Alliance had discussed how to respond, and the final consensus was to adhere to the five major goals.

「結束一黨專政」是否受言論自由保障？

The prosecution argued that freedom of speech is not absolute, and that the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" with the intent to incite the audience to subvert the regime had crossed the line of human rights protection.

Lee Cheuk-yan's team pointed out that Article 41 of the Chinese Constitution protects citizens' right to criticise any state organ, including the Communist Party, and the Alliance had never called on people to use any means, including illegal means, to end the dictatorship. Merely chanting slogans and making political demands should be protected by freedom of speech. Chow Hang-tung also said that in a society that respects freedom of speech, advocating political reform and criticising government actions is normal and necessary, and the speech in question seeks to restrict and monitor power. Even if it is unpopular with the government, the court must be vigilant against the government's overreach in restricting speech.

During the trial, there was discussion of whether the defendants' support for Liu Xiaobo and the Charter 08 he initiated, and supporting people doing things that might invite criminal liability in mainland China, constituted "illegal means" under the subversive charge.

煽惑人違反內地法律是否違國安法？

Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung mentioned in their testimony that they supported Charter 08 initiated by Liu Xiaobo and others. The judge was concerned about whether the defendants were supporting people in doing things that could attract criminal liability in mainland China, and noted that "illegal means" in the subversive charge meant being illegal in Hong Kong or mainland China, and that this should be addressed in submissions.

However, Lee Cheuk-yan's team questioned that the prosecution's basis of prosecution was violation of the Constitution, and had never mentioned that "violating domestic criminal law" was illegal means. Illegal means should only involve Hong Kong law, and whether the defendants incited people to use means violating mainland criminal law to promote constitutional amendment should not be an issue in this case. The prosecution also clarified that "illegal means" only targeted violation of the Chinese Constitution, not criminal law, and that the inciting act must occur in Hong Kong. The defendants had to issue the inciting message in Hong Kong, with the recipients being Hong Kong people receiving it in Hong Kong. It only needed to be proven that the recipients received the inciting message; even if they did not carry out the incited act, the charge could be proven.
